item.aggregated_output:
Read /Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation/enrichment/bible/work/s103/discovery/s103-20261009/sec15/luna/package.md. It holds image section 15 (Buluşmalar) of the frozen surah commentary of surah 103: the Arabic text of the ayat concerned, the Turkish
commentary written on them, the words/roots/branch labels recorded in the frozen surah commentary, and the
whole surah in Arabic. The selected commentary defines your scope; the other inputs supply context.

Find, from the Hebrew Bible, the New Testament, and the Jewish and Christian literature around them (Targum,
Mishnah, Talmud, midrash, pseudepigrapha, Christian apocrypha, Church Fathers, Syriac homilies), every text an
advanced reader of this commentary should have beside it. Judge each text on what it says in its own place, not
on resemblance of a word. Weigh at least:

- paralel: the same figure, scene or story told in the other scripture;
- motif: a shared image, formula, liturgical act or ethical motif without a shared story;
- karsi_anlati: the Qur'an tells it differently, corrects or answers it; the difference is the point;
- soydas: a Hebrew, Aramaic or Syriac cognate of a key word of these ayat and how the other scripture uses it;
- yorum_gelenegi: Jewish or Christian interpretation of a parallel text that changes what the parallel means.

Before grading, work through every distinct scene, object, action, relation, formula and secondary sense
actually developed in the commentary, including any v16 augment additions. Recall direct formulations, repeated
occurrences, nonlexical parallels, relevant reversals and interpretive traditions. Do not let the title, first
scene or already quoted passages stand in for the whole page. For a Buluşmalar section, consider the particular
meetings between images its prose develops. Root/branch labels are not dictionary definitions, evidence of
cognacy or permission to import an undeveloped sense. Do this review internally; output only candidate rows.

Use the package's Semitic root table: for every Arabic root it lists, recall how the corresponding Hebrew or
Aramaic root is used across the Hebrew Bible, passages that play on the same consonants, and passages whose
wording shows a difference from what the ayah says. Propose such passages as soydas (shared root), motif,
paralel or karsi_anlati as fits, and name the basis in `basis` (the root, and whether it is the table's sound
correspondence or your own recollection). Same consonants with an unrelated sense are not a connection.

Every explanation must identify a particular detail or claim in the commentary, the corresponding detail in
the candidate's own context, and what the relationship adds. Shared vocabulary, a broad religious theme or
the same speaker alone is insufficient. Do not invent imagery that neither text supports. A shared word is
not required. Preserve indirect, secondary and contrary readings with a concrete connection; do not choose
one preferred reading. A parallel is not a dependence: say what the texts share, not who borrowed.

Check the speaker, addressee, action, negation and verse boundary in remembered context. Name a neighbouring
verse separately when its own contribution is necessary; proximity alone does not qualify it. Keep Hebrew,
Aramaic, Syriac and Greek quotations short and specific to the cited passage and witness. If exact wording or
numbering is uncertain, explain the connection and uncertainty in English instead of reconstructing a quote.
Label roots, dictionary forms and wording from the source commentary explicitly. Never combine verses into
one quotation. Distinguish WLC's written/ketiv stream from qere and other readings; name another witness when
you rely on it. Discovery is memory-only: the later verifier will open the actual texts and check your claims.

Include every candidate meeting this standard. There is no target list length. Strong means a direct,
specific correspondence, including a secondary feature developed in the prose. Medium means a specific
correspondence with an explicit interpretive bridge. Weak means a plausible, specific connection whose
uncertainty you identify; it still cannot be generic. Counter-narrative is a relationship kind, not weaker
confidence. Model agreement and a follow-up origin never make a claim verified.

Write one TSV row per distinct connection with exactly six tab-separated fields:

strength	tradition	kind	ref	basis	short_explanation

strength: strong, medium, weak. tradition: tevrat (Hebrew Bible and Jewish literature) or incil (New Testament and
Christian literature). kind: paralel, motif, karsi_anlati, soydas, yorum_gelenegi. ref: for the Hebrew Bible and
the New Testament an edition-qualified OSIS reference, one verse per row, no ranges
(WLC:Gen.22.2, WLC:Ps.1.3, SBLGNT:Matt.6.5; consecutive verses on their own rows).
Use Hebrew WLC numbering for Hebrew Bible candidates and SBLGNT numbering for New Testament candidates;
do not silently transfer English/KJV verse numbers. For other works give the work and its place as a reader
cites it (Targum Jonathan on Genesis 22:2;
Genesis Rabbah 56:1; Berakhot 60b; Ephrem, Hymns on Paradise 5:6; Protevangelium of James 8). basis: the words,
scene or motif that carries the link, in a few words. Strongest first. Keep distinct reasons or link kinds for
one passage in separate rows; exact repeated connections are unnecessary. Do not regrade an existing row.
The handoff groups references but preserves each distinct connection for an individual verdict.

Do not write a header row, rank numbers, Markdown, sections or prose outside TSV rows. Save the rows to
/Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation/enrichment/bible/work/s103/discovery/s103-20261009/sec15/luna/list.tsv. End nonempty files with a newline. Zero qualifying candidates means an explicitly created
empty file. The saved file, not the chat response, is the deliverable.
# S103: image section 15 (Buluşmalar) of the frozen surah commentary

## Ayat (Arabic)

103:1	وَٱلْعَصْرِ
103:2	إِنَّ ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ لَفِى خُسْرٍ
103:3	إِلَّا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ وَعَمِلُوا۟ ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتِ وَتَوَاصَوْا۟ بِٱلْحَقِّ وَتَوَاصَوْا۟ بِٱلصَّبْرِ

## Words, roots and branches named by the frozen surah commentary

These are source labels, not dictionary definitions or verified cross-language cognates.

ayah	word	root	branch	image
(No lexical members recorded for this target.)

## Semitic root table (Hebrew and Biblical Aramaic correspondences of the Arabic roots above)

Generated by enrichment/bible/hebrew.py from the Open Scriptures lexicon and the WLC lemmas. A regular sound
correspondence is a candidate, not proof of cognacy; "BDB cites an Arabic cognate" is the lexicon's own note.

(The frozen text of this target cites no Arabic root.)

## Frozen commentary (Turkish)

İmgeler birkaç sahnede üst üste biner. En geniş olanı yaşlı adamın bahçesidir {source:2:266}: hurma ve üzüm, yani sıkılacak meyve; yağmurla büyüyen ürün; ömrün geç vakti, yani asrın akşamüstü anlamı; ve sonunda aynı kökten bir kasırga. Bir ömür boyunca biriken ürünün, tam elde edileceği vakitte, sıkmanın ve yağmurun adını taşıyan kökün öteki yüzüyle yok olması, ikinci ayetin kaybını tek bir görüntüye toplar. Yusuf'un yılı ise aynı kökün iyi yüzlerini birleştirir: {ar:فِيهِ يُغَاثُ ٱلنَّاسُ وَفِيهِ يَعْصِرُونَ, tr:fîhi yugâsu'n-nâsu ve fîhi ya'sirûn, gloss:o yıl insanlar yardıma kavuşur ve o yıl sıkarlar, source:12:49}; yağmur, sıkma ve kurtuluş aynı cümlededir. Yusuf'un zindanında ise sıkma ile alıkonma yan yanadır {source:12:36}, ve sabrın kendisi, acı bir sıkma özü olarak, alıkonmanın kelimesiyle aynıdır.

İkinci sahne yokuştur. Sarp yokuşa atılmak {source:90:11} bir yolculuk ve bir yük sahnesidir; yokuşun ne olduğu sorulunca {ar:فَكُّ رَقَبَةٍ, tr:fekku rakabe, gloss:bir boynu çözmek, source:90:13} ve {ar:أَوْ إِطْعَٰمٌۭ فِى يَوْمٍۢ ذِى مَسْغَبَةٍۢ, tr:ev it'âmun fî yevmin zî mesgabe, gloss:ya da açlık gününde doyurmak, source:90:14} cevabı gelir; tutulan esir çözülür. Ardından karşılıklı tavsiye gelir {source:90:17}. Yük hayvanı ve yol, tutma ve salıverme, çekişmeden birlikteliğe geçiş tek bir yürüyüşte birleşir; bu, surenin üçüncü ayetindeki fiilin Kur'an'daki öteki kullanımıdır.

Üçüncü sahne vasiyet anıdır {source:5:106}: ölüm, alıkonma, yemin, vasiyet ve hak aynı ayettedir; ertesi ayette tanıklığın "daha hak" oluşu tartılır {source:5:107}. Burada tutma imgesi ile emanet imgesi buluşur, borç ayetinde de pazar ile emanet buluşur {source:2:282}. Kötü pazarlık ile ters sabır da tek ayettedir {source:2:175}: sapıklığı satın alanlar, ateşe dayanan cüretkârlardır. Tutunma ile birliktelik ise ip ayetinde birleşir {source:3:103}: hep birlikte tutunmak, düşmanların kardeş olması ve uçurumun kenarından çekilmek bir sahnedir. Örümcek evi hem sığınağın hem dokumanın karşıtıdır {source:29:41}. Soyların kesildiği an ile terazinin hafif gelmesi de art arda gelir {source:23:101}.

Bu buluşmalar surenin hareketini taşır. Birinci ayet tek kelimeyle, sıkan, saran, bağlayan ve harcanan bir zamanı anar: hem sermaye hem günün sonu, hem sıkma hem sığınak, hem yağmur hem kasırga. İkinci ayet bu zamanın içindeki insanı gösterir: ana parası eriyen, sapan, kendini tutamayan, terazide hafif gelen biri. Üçüncü ayet sahneyi tek kişiden topluluğa çevirir: iman edenler güvenliğe girer, işleri kerpiç gibi yerine oturur, birbirlerine gece ile gündüz gibi eklenirler ve el değiştiren iki şey vardır. Hak, hem borç hem sapmayan darbe hem de herkesi işiyle yüzleştiren gündür; sabır hem kendini tutmak hem kefil hem de mühürlü kapta saklanan acı ilaçtır. Sure baskı ve tükenişle açılır, birbirine iletilen ve saklanan bir özle kapanır.

## Whole surah (Arabic)

103:1	وَٱلْعَصْرِ
103:2	إِنَّ ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ لَفِى خُسْرٍ
103:3	إِلَّا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ وَعَمِلُوا۟ ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتِ وَتَوَاصَوْا۟ بِٱلْحَقِّ وَتَوَاصَوْا۟ بِٱلصَّبْرِ

/bin/bash -lc "cat > /Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation/enrichment/bible/work/s103/discovery/s103-20261009/sec15/luna/list.tsv <<'LUNA_TSV'
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Gen.40.11	Joseph in prison; grapes pressed into Pharaoh’s cup	The commentary joins Joseph’s confinement to pressing; in Joseph’s prison story the cupbearer dreams of squeezing grapes into Pharaoh’s cup, while the dream belongs to the cupbearer.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Gen.41.48	Joseph stores the abundant harvest	The commentary’s Yusuf year makes relief follow scarcity; Genesis has Joseph gather the abundant years’ produce into storehouses so the later famine can be survived.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ps.105.18	Joseph fettered	The commentary pairs Joseph’s imprisonment with patience; the psalm retelling puts his feet in fetters and his neck in iron, making confinement part of the Joseph story.
strong	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Ps.105.19	Joseph tested while awaiting the promise	The commentary makes patience meet detention; the next line of the psalm says the Lord’s word tested Joseph until its fulfillment, giving his confinement a waiting-for-release dimension.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.12.20	Stored harvest interrupted by death	The commentary’s aged gardener loses the yield before enjoying it; Jesus’ rich farmer plans many years around his abundant stores, then is told that his life ends that night.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.18.17	Merchants’ wealth lost in one hour	The commentary compresses accumulated produce and capital into sudden loss; Revelation says Babylon’s great wealth is laid waste in one hour, as merchants watch their trade collapse.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Jas.5.7	Crop, rain, and patience	The commentary joins rain, fruit, and sabr; James tells the farmer to wait patiently for the precious crop until it receives the early and late rains, making delay before yield the point.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.90.6	Life flourishes, then withers at evening	The commentary reads asr as the evening of a life; the psalm compares human flourishing to grass that sprouts in the morning and withers by evening.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.90.10	Brief lifespan and toil	The commentary makes a lifetime’s yield vulnerable at its late hour; the psalm counts human years as short and full of toil, then quickly gone.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.12.2	Light and rain clouds dim before old age	The commentary layers life’s late afternoon with rain and its destructive turn; Ecclesiastes pictures sun, moon, and stars darkening and clouds returning after rain in its approach to death.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.92.14	Fruit still borne in old age	The commentary’s old owner loses his garden as age advances; the psalm instead pictures the righteous still bearing fruit in old age, a concrete counter-image of fruitful late life.
strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah Avot 2:15	Short day, much work, pressing master	The commentary treats time as expiring capital and deeds as urgent; Tarfon says the day is short, the work abundant, and the Master of the House presses, joining time, labor, and accountability.
strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah Avot 2:16	Do not desist from unfinished work	The commentary’s closing community keeps transmitting good action within limited time; Tarfon says one need not finish the work but is not free to desist, adding persistence without claiming control of the outcome.
strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah Peah 1:1	Good deeds as fruit and principal	The commentary makes good works the lasting yield of time; Peah says certain deeds bear fruit in this world while their principal remains for the world to come, an explicit investment image.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.58.6	Release the bound and break the yoke	The commentary defines the steep ascent through freeing a captive; Isaiah’s fast is to loose wicked bonds, undo the yoke, and let the oppressed go free.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.58.7	Give bread to the hungry	The commentary names feeding on a day of hunger as part of the ascent; Isaiah places sharing bread with the hungry in the same account of true fasting.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.23.5	Lift an enemy’s overloaded donkey	The commentary moves from struggle toward companionship and mentions a beast of burden; Torah commands helping even an enemy’s donkey rise under its load, making cooperation concrete.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.10.34	A wounded traveler carried on an animal	The commentary’s road and burden imagery turns toward care; the Samaritan binds the robbed traveler’s wounds and places him on his own animal, converting a dangerous road encounter into help.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.25.35	Feed the hungry	The commentary makes feeding the hungry part of the difficult ascent; in Jesus’ judgment scene, feeding the hungry is named as a deed by which people answer the king.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.25.36	Visit the imprisoned	The commentary pairs release from captivity with feeding; Jesus’ judgment scene separately names visiting a person in prison, connecting practical care to final reckoning.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.12.20	Feed an enemy	The commentary’s movement from enmity to fellowship has a concrete ethic in Paul’s instruction to feed a hungry enemy, answering hostility with care.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Gal.6.2	Bear one another’s burdens	The commentary turns from the isolated person to mutual counsel; Paul tells the community to carry one another’s burdens, making shared endurance an enacted duty.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.4.10	A companion lifts the fallen	The commentary’s steep path and transition into togetherness meet Ecclesiastes’ image of one companion raising another who falls on the road of life.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.4.12	A cord holds companions together	The commentary reads holding together as rescue from danger; Ecclesiastes says a three-strand cord is not quickly broken, giving the communal bond a material image.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.19.15	Two or three witnesses establish a matter	The commentary’s deathbed bequest depends on witnesses; Deuteronomy likewise rejects a single witness and requires two or three for a charge.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Lev.5.1	Witness called under oath	The commentary gathers oath, testimony, and truth at the moment of a bequest; Leviticus treats hearing a public oath and withholding testimony as a legal offense.
strong	incil	yorum_gelenegi	SBLGNT:Heb.9.16	Death activates a will or covenant	The commentary’s death-triggered bequest meets Hebrews’ use of Greek diathēkē as a will: the writer uses the testator’s death to explain how the covenant takes effect.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Jer.32.10	Signed deed, witnesses, and weighed silver	The commentary says the debt scene joins market and trust; Jeremiah records a land purchase with a signed deed, witnesses, and silver weighed out, a close transactional analogue.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Jer.32.14	Sealed deeds kept in an earthen vessel	The commentary joins financial trust to preserved contents; Jeremiah orders sealed and open copies of the deed stored in a jar so they last, showing custody protecting a transaction.
strong	tevrat	motif	Sirach 29:3	Promise and honesty in lending	The commentary brings debt together with trust; Sirach tells a lender to keep a promise and deal faithfully with the borrower, making reliability part of credit.
strong	tevrat	motif	Shabbat 31a	Faithful business dealings at judgment	The commentary joins market trust to the day when deeds are faced; the Talmud’s first judgment question is whether one dealt faithfully in business.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.16.11	Faithfulness with wealth and entrusted riches	The commentary’s debt verse brings commerce and trust together; Jesus asks who will entrust true riches to someone unfaithful with worldly wealth.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Phlm.1.18	Another’s debt charged to Paul	The commentary’s testament and debt scenes make obligation transferable; Paul tells Philemon to charge any debt or wrong by Onesimus to him.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Phlm.1.19	A written promise to repay	The commentary joins a financial obligation to trust; Paul says he writes in his own hand that he will repay, turning personal assurance into a written pledge.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.27.6	A friend’s wounds can be faithful	The commentary lets truth be a straight, painful blow; Proverbs says a friend’s wounds may be trusted, presenting frank correction as a form of loyalty.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Zech.8.16	Speak truth to one another	The commentary’s mutual counsel is centered on truth; Zechariah commands neighbors to speak truth and render judgments that make for peace.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Eph.4.25	Truth spoken among interdependent members	The commentary turns truth into reciprocal counsel within a community; Paul says to speak truth with one’s neighbor because members belong to one another.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Tim.2.2	Entrusted teaching passed to further teachers	The commentary ends with truth and patience changing hands; Paul tells Timothy to entrust what he heard to faithful people able to teach others, an explicit chain of transmission.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Thess.5.14	Encourage the weak and be patient with all	The commentary’s community counsels patience; Paul joins encouraging the fainthearted and helping the weak to the instruction to be patient with everyone.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.10.24	Provoke one another to good works	The commentary makes mutual counsel issue in righteous action; Hebrews says to consider how to spur one another toward love and good works.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.3.13	The Day tests each person’s work	The commentary imagines deeds fitting like building material and truth as the day of reckoning; Paul says the Day reveals each builder’s work and fire tests it.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Pet.2.5	People built together as living stones	The commentary pictures righteous action as bricks set in place; Peter calls believers living stones being built into a spiritual house, making the community itself constructed.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Eph.4.16	Each part builds the whole body	The commentary’s believers add to one another; Paul’s body is joined through each supporting part and builds itself up in love.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.12.25	Members care for one another	The commentary’s mutual counsel makes the group interdependent; Paul says the body’s members should have the same care for one another.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.16.32	Patience as rule over oneself	The commentary reads sabr as self-restraint; Proverbs says ruling one’s spirit is greater than taking a city, making inner restraint the achievement.
strong	tevrat	motif	Sirach 2:4	Patience in adversity	The commentary treats patience as something retained through hardship; Sirach tells the faithful to accept what befalls them and be patient in humiliation.
strong	tevrat	motif	Sirach 2:5	Faithfulness tested like gold in fire	The commentary’s patience has a bitter, fiery trial aspect; Sirach says the faithful are tested in the furnace of humiliation as gold is tested in fire.
strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Dan.3.18	Faithfulness chosen despite the furnace	The commentary calls condemned people’s readiness for fire a perverse patience; Daniel’s three youths accept the possibility of fire rather than worship another god, reversing what endurance serves.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.12.14	Every deed brought into judgment	The commentary says the day makes each person face their work; Ecclesiastes says every deed, including what is hidden, comes into judgment.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Dan.5.27	Weighed and found wanting	The commentary links severed kinship to scales that come up light; Daniel’s wall-writing scene weighs a king and finds him wanting, making weight a verdict on conduct.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ezek.14.20	Righteousness cannot be transferred to a child	The commentary places severed kinship beside individual weighing; Ezekiel says even Noah, Daniel, and Job could save only themselves, not sons or daughters, so family ties do not transfer standing.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.2.6	Each repaid according to deeds	The commentary says the day confronts everyone with their work; Paul states that God repays each person according to deeds.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.20.12	The dead judged by recorded deeds	The commentary joins the loss of kinship with personal weighing; Revelation depicts the dead judged from books according to what they had done.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.14.12	A seemingly right road ends in death	The commentary describes the human as straying within time; Proverbs warns that a way can seem right yet end in death, specifying the danger of misjudgment.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Mark.8.36	Profit that costs one’s life	The commentary describes human life as capital that can melt into loss; Jesus asks what is gained by acquiring the whole world if one forfeits oneself.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Jas.4.13	A year of trade and expected profit	The commentary treats time as capital; James depicts merchants planning a year in a city to trade and make profit, exposing life’s plans to uncertainty.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Jas.4.14	Life as a passing mist	The commentary reads the time of a human life as brief and vulnerable; James calls life a vapor that appears briefly and then vanishes.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Gal.6.9	Patient good work bears a later harvest	The commentary closes with deeds and patience transmitted together; Paul urges persistence in doing good because a harvest comes in its season if people do not give up.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Pet.1.6	Self-control and endurance after faith	The commentary’s believers join faith to good action and sabr; Peter’s sequence adds self-control and endurance to faith-informed virtue.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.14.12	Faithful community defined by endurance	The commentary gathers belief, right action, and patience in a community; Revelation names the saints’ endurance together with keeping God’s commands and faith in Jesus.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.7.31	The world’s form is passing away	The commentary treats time and worldly capital as expiring; Paul tells believers to use the world without clinging to it because its present form is passing.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.6.19	Earthly treasure can be destroyed or stolen	The commentary’s accumulated fruit and capital remain vulnerable; Jesus warns that earthly stores are exposed to moth, corrosion, and thieves.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.5.2	Vineyard, grapes, and winepress	The commentary’s garden contains grapes and fruit meant for pressing; Isaiah’s cultivated vineyard has a winepress prepared for its expected grapes, though its yield proves different.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.5.6	A vineyard ruined when rain is withheld	The commentary’s garden is destroyed by a sudden storm after fruitfulness; Isaiah instead makes a failed vineyard waste and withholds rain, a distinct judgment pattern.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.1.19	A violent wind destroys a house amid accumulated loss	The commentary makes a whirlwind erase what was gathered; Job’s children die when a great wind collapses the house during their feast, after earlier losses of property.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Hag.1.6	Wages vanish into a bag with holes	The commentary says human capital melts away; Haggai pictures earned wages disappearing into a bag with holes, tying loss to futile labor.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.5.13	Wealth perishes in a bad venture	The commentary’s garden loses its accumulated yield at the moment of expectation; Ecclesiastes describes wealth kept to its owner’s hurt and lost through a disastrous venture.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.23.5	Wealth grows wings and flies away	The commentary makes stored capital vulnerable to sudden disappearance; Proverbs pictures riches sprouting wings and flying off, turning possession into impermanence.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.11.4	Riches fail on the day of wrath	The commentary contrasts loss with deeds that carry a person through judgment; Proverbs says riches cannot deliver on the day of wrath but righteousness delivers from death.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.37.21	Borrowing without repayment	The commentary links debt to trust; the psalm contrasts a wicked borrower who does not repay with a righteous person who gives generously.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.15.2	Release of debts	The commentary develops debt as one face of truth; Deuteronomy commands release of loans at the appointed remission, connecting obligation to mercy within the community.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.11.1	Honest weights in trade	The commentary brings market trust and truthful judgment together; Proverbs condemns false scales and approves accurate weights in commerce.
medium	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Matt.5.34	A general ban on swearing	The commentary’s witness scene uses an oath to establish a bequest; Jesus’ sermon tells disciples not to swear, giving a contrasting ethic for truthful speech.
